America has pretty much everything in abundance. Harvesting of resources is mostly a factor of economics and not availability.

Rare earths, for example, are not actually rare. The Chinese dominate the market currently because they produce them cheaper, with low cost labor and low environmental regulations. The Chinese are also currently the largest buyer, as rare earths are used mainly in manufacturing. You can expect this landscape to change under the new trading system.

Also important to understand is that a large percentage of precious metals are actually produced as a byproduct of other mining processes. A nickle mine, for example, also produces gold, silver, etc. Metals tend to be found in the immediate vicinity of other metals. Such is the nature of volcanism, and how metals are deposited in the earth.

How much effort any particular harvesting process puts into secondary harvesting of other metals present in the production stream is also mainly a factor of economics. If a profit can be made by further harvesting the secondary materials, say to extract the gold along with the primary nickle extraction, then often the investment will be made to do so.

Half of all global silver is produced as a secondary extraction process in other mining.

So, when the economy is bad, and miners reduce the production of primary metals, then precious metal production is also reduced as the mine goes quiet. In a good economy the opposite is true.

The truth is there is known gold, and every other metal... known deposits all over the place. Harvesting of these deposits depends mainly on price, and price is ruled mainly by demand. A spike in demand brings greater production online, after a lag period including what appears to be a sustained price increase.

The current spike in gold prices is significant, but probably hasn't been sustained for long enough to convince investors to risk additional money to bring closed mines back online, or to invest more heavily in extracting gold from existing production. The current price hikes can be seen as a temporary market aberration resulting from the trade negotiations. What happens to the gold price if Trump and China finally make a deal, say in three months from now? Then gold falls back to $1200, you can't recover your investment, and your company goes bankrupt. See the problem?

Making decisions now is pure gambling. Larger companies can afford to make bigger gambles, and have more resources to survive mistakes. Small companies go under if they guess wrong. They cannot survive the financial costs of making a mistake.

Most investors prefer a sure thing. For example, if it appears certain that trade talks with China have completely collapsed, and a full American pull out is assured, then you will see very heavy investment in American mining companies, bringing those companies back online to fill the void.
